title: The Temple
alternative_titles: The Temple: Sacred Poems and Private Ejaculations
description: George Herbert's posthumous collection of 160 English religious poems, arranged in three parts — 'The Church-Porch', 'The Church', and 'The Church Militant' — which renders the life of the soul and the parish in an extraordinary variety of forms, from pattern poems to hymns and dramatic soliloquies.
plot_or_argument: 'The Church-Porch' gives moral precepts to a young man; 'The Church' traces the soul's struggles with God through poems of sin, affliction, love, and consolation ('The Collar', 'The Pulley', 'Love III'); 'The Church Militant' is a prophetic vision of the church's corruption and the spread of true religion westward.
narrative_structure: A tripartite collection with the shape of a spiritual autobiography, moving from moral instruction through the drama of devotion to eschatological prophecy.
principal_characters: the poet-priest; God; the soul; the Church
meter_and_prosody: A prodigious variety of stanza forms, shaped and pattern poems ('Easter Wings', 'The Altar'), concrete imagery, and colloquial rhythm in the service of devotion.
historical_context: Herbert sent the manuscript to Nicholas Ferrar of Little Gidding shortly before his death in 1633, asking him to publish it if he thought it might 'turn to the advantage of any dejected poor soul'; it was printed at Cambridge in 1633 and became a devotional best-seller.
literary_significance: The Temple is the supreme work of English devotional verse, fusing metaphysical wit with Anglican humility; it shaped religious poetry from Vaughan and Crashaw to Coleridge, Eliot, and Heaney.
bibliographical_notes: First printed 1633. Standard edition: The English Poems of George Herbert (Helen Wilcox, ed., Cambridge University Press, 2007).

title: A Priest to the Temple
description: Herbert's prose manual of pastoral practice, written for the guidance of country clergy; in short chapters it describes the parson's character, duties, preaching, catechising, visiting, and conduct, presenting the ideal of the devoted, humble, and practical parish priest.
plot_or_argument: Each chapter ('The Parson's Character', 'The Parson Preaching', 'The Parson in Circuits', etc.) offers practical and spiritual counsel, arguing that the parson must know and love his flock, teach plainly, and sanctify every part of life.
narrative_structure: A series of short prose chapters forming a complete guide to the pastoral office.
meter_and_prosody: Plain, homely, wise prose with occasional proverbial turns and scriptural allusion.
historical_context: Written c. 1632 at Bemerton and circulated in manuscript; published in 1652 as part of Herbert's Remains, it reflects the Laudian and practical devotional ideals of the Caroline church.
literary_significance: A classic of Anglican pastoral literature, valued for its humane wisdom and its influence on Izaak Walton's Life of Herbert and on the ideal of the country parson in English letters.
bibliographical_notes: First printed 1652. Standard edition: The Works of George Herbert (John N. Wall and others, eds.).

title: Silex Scintillans
alternative_titles: Silex Scintillans; or, Sacred Poems and Private Ejaculations
description: Henry Vaughan's great collection of mystical religious verse (1650, expanded 1655), whose poems seek God through nature, childhood memory, and visionary longing — 'The Retreat', 'The World', 'Peace', and the 'Rules and Lessons' — earning him the title 'the Silurist' and a place among the metaphysical poets.
plot_or_argument: The poems move between longing for a lost innocence and eternity glimpsed behind the world ('Eternity' in 'The World'), meditations on scripture and the sacraments, elegies, and practical rules for holy living.
narrative_structure: A two-part collection (1650, then 1655 with 'Flamma sine Fumo') of devotional lyrics, translations, and epigrams loosely ordered around themes of nature, eternity, and faith.
principal_characters: the poet; God; the soul; natural and biblical figures
meter_and_prosody: Luminous, musical verse with emblematic structure and a visionary intensity drawn from Herbert but wilder and more personal.
historical_context: Written in the aftermath of the Civil Wars and Vaughan's royalist seclusion in Breconshire, and deeply influenced by Herbert's Temple; the 1655 edition added secular and satirical pieces.
literary_significance: Once obscure, Silex Scintillans was recovered by the Romantics and Coleridge (whose 'intimation of immortality' echoes 'The Retreat') and is now recognised as major mystical poetry of the seventeenth century.
attribution_notes: Uncontested; published under the initials 'H.V.' and the title 'the Silurist'.
bibliographical_notes: First edition 1650, expanded 1655. Standard edition: The Works of Henry Vaughan (F. E. Hutchinson, ed., Clarendon Press, 1914).

title: Olor Iscanus
alternative_titles: Olor Iscanus: The Swan of Usk
description: A collection of Vaughan's earlier secular and occasional verse, published by his brother William in 1651 against the poet's wish, including love poems, elegies, satires, epigrams, and translations of Boethius, The Distichs of Cato, and Casimire Sarbiewski.
plot_or_argument: The volume gathers Vaughan's pre-conversion and secular work — amatory and elegiac poems, versions of Ovid and Ausonius, the satirical 'Time' poems, and pious translations — representing the literary range before his mystical turn.
narrative_structure: A miscellaneous collection of secular lyrics, translations, and epigrams without a unifying sequence.
meter_and_prosody: Varied lyric meters; translation in verse; a more worldly, sometimes uneven, manner than Silex Scintillans.
historical_context: Composed largely in the 1640s; Vaughan suppressed it, but his twin brother Thomas's death and William's initiative led to its publication in 1651, dedicated with the 'swan of Usk' emblem of the river on which Vaughan lived.
literary_significance: Important for understanding Vaughan's development and his classical and secular range, and as a document of royalist literary culture during the Interregnum.
attribution_notes: Uncontested; published by Vaughan's brother against his expressed preference.
bibliographical_notes: First printed 1651. Standard edition: The Works of Henry Vaughan (F. E. Hutchinson, ed., Clarendon Press, 1914).

title: Steps to the Temple
alternative_titles: Steps to the Temple: Sacred Poems with Other Delights of the Muses
description: Richard Crashaw's first English collection (1646), containing his religious epigrams, hymns, and translations, including the famous 'The Weeper' on Mary Magdalene, 'Musicks Duell', versions of Marino, and sacred epigrams — the baroque, sensuous devotional verse that distinguishes him among the metaphysicals.
plot_or_argument: The poems celebrate the saints and sacraments and the mysteries of faith in ecstatic, image-laden verse, turning epigrammatic wit and continental baroque conceit to Catholic-inflected devotion.
narrative_structure: A collection of sacred epigrams, hymns, elegies, and translations, framed by a commendatory poem on Herbert's Temple.
principal_characters: Mary Magdalene; the Virgin; Christ; the saints
meter_and_prosody: Elaborate, musical, sometimes extravagant conceits; epigrammatic compression; a lush, sensual baroque style.
historical_context: Published in London in 1646 while Crashaw was an Anglican; he converted to Catholicism and went into exile, and a further collection, Carmen Deo Nostro, appeared in Paris in 1652.
literary_significance: 'The Weeper' and the sacred epigrams are among the most striking religious lyrics of the century, admired by Cowley and later critics for their daring imagery and fervour.
bibliographical_notes: First printed 1646, enlarged 1648. Standard edition: The Poems English, Latin and Greek of Richard Crashaw (L. C. Martin, ed.).

title: Carmen Deo Nostro
alternative_titles: Carmen Deo Nostro, Te Decet Hymnus, Sacred Poems
description: Crashaw's posthumous Catholic collection, published in Paris in 1652 with an emblematic frontispiece of the crucifix, containing his mature hymns — including the great 'Hymn in Adoration of the Blessed Sacrament' and the hymns to St Teresa — in an ecstatic, baroque devotion.
plot_or_argument: The hymns celebrate Catholic doctrine (the Eucharist, the Name of Jesus, the saints, St Teresa's mystical ecstasy) in fervent, sensuous verse marked by paradox, repetition, and intense religious feeling.
narrative_structure: A collection of hymns, epigrams, and religious verse with emblematic apparatus, unified by Catholic devotional subjects.
principal_characters: Christ; the Virgin; St Teresa; the saints
meter_and_prosody: Musical, incantatory verse with baroque repetition and paradox; emblematic and visionary imagery.
historical_context: Written after Crashaw's conversion and exile; published at Loreto/Paris in 1652, three years after his death, by his friend Thomas Carre, with the poet's own drawings.
literary_significance: The principal English work of Catholic baroque devotion, its hymn to St Teresa and 'Adoration of the Blessed Sacrament' are among the most ecstatic religious poems in English.
bibliographical_notes: First printed Paris, 1652. Standard edition: The Poems English, Latin and Greek of Richard Crashaw (L. C. Martin, ed.).

title: Centuries of Thankfulness
description: Thomas Traherne's great mystical prose meditations — four 'centuries' of numbered paragraphs celebrating God's goodness, the soul's felicity, and the wonder of creation as apprehended by an innocent eye — unpublished in his lifetime and discovered and printed only in the early twentieth century.
plot_or_argument: The Centuries argue that true happiness consists in rightly valuing and enjoying God's creation, recover the infant soul's vision of infinity, and exhort gratitude and thanksgiving as the path to felicity.
narrative_structure: Four 'centuries' of 100 numbered meditative paragraphs each (partly incomplete), forming a cumulative rhapsody of wonder and thanksgiving.
principal_characters: the soul; God; the self in childhood
meter_and_prosody: Rhapsodic, cumulative, rhythmic prose of wonder, with visionary imagery of light, infinity, and childhood.
historical_context: Written in the early 1670s and left in manuscript; misattributed to Henry Vaughan until Bertram Dobell acquired and published them in 1908, revealing a major unknown mystic.
literary_significance: The Centuries are a unique achievement in English mystical prose, anticipating Romantic celebrations of childhood vision and influencing later spiritual and literary writers.
attribution_notes: Uncontested once Dobell established Traherne's authorship; the manuscripts were long misattributed to Vaughan.
bibliographical_notes: First published 1908 (Dobell). Standard edition: Centuries of Thankfulness (Denise Inge or the Oxford/Clarendon editions).

title: Roman Forgeries
alternative_titles: Roman Forgeries: Giving an Account of False Records
description: Traherne's only work published in his lifetime: an anti-Catholic polemic exposing spurious documents and legends in Roman tradition (the Donation of Constantine, fictitious councils and decrees), arguing for Protestantism on grounds of historical truth.
plot_or_argument: Traherne catalogues and refutes alleged forgeries and false records in the Roman church's history, contending that the truth of a religion can be tested by the authenticity of its documents and tradition.
narrative_structure: A polemical treatise of historical argument and refutation.
meter_and_prosody: Argumentative, learned prose of controversial divinity.
historical_context: Published in 1673 amid the anti-Catholic controversies that preceded the Popish Plot and the Exclusion Crisis, reflecting Traherne's Anglican commitment.
literary_significance: Important as Traherne's only lifetime publication and as a document of seventeenth-century anti-Catholic polemic; it contrasts with his unpublished mystical writings.
bibliographical_notes: Published 1673. Standard edition: The Works of Thomas Traherne (Centenary Edition, D. S. Thomson and others, eds.).

title: Davideis
alternative_titles: Davideis: A Sacred Poem of the Troubles of David
description: Abraham Cowley's unfinished biblical epic in four books (in Poems, 1656), retelling the persecution of David by Saul in heroic couplets, with a preface defending the modern epic and arguing for a Christian verse built on rhyme rather than Milton's blank verse.
plot_or_argument: The poem narrates David's flight and troubles under Saul's jealous pursuit, drawing on the books of Samuel, with digressions and a prefatory argument on epic theory and the state of English poetry.
narrative_structure: A heroic epic in rhymed couplets (four books of a planned twelve), with a critical preface on epic conventions.
meter_and_prosody: Closed heroic couplets, which Cowley advocated against rhymeless verse in his preface.
historical_context: Published in 1656 during the Interregnum; its preface engages the debate about epic form and the future of English poetry that Milton would answer with Paradise Lost's blank verse.
literary_significance: An influential, if unfinished, attempt at a modern Christian epic, important for its couplet form and its theory of epic, and as a foil to Milton's practice.
bibliographical_notes: Published in Poems (1656). Standard edition: The Essays and Other Prose Writings / Poems of Abraham Cowley (A. B. Gough, ed., Oxford).

title: Pindarique Odes
description: The odes in Cowley's Poems (1656) that established the loose, irregular 'Pindaric' form in English — ambitious, varied-line odes on great subjects, including 'The Muse', 'To Mr Hobs' (Thomas Hobbes), and 'The Plagues of Egypt' — which became a major vehicle for Restoration and Augustan poetry.
plot_or_argument: The odes treat poetry and its critics, philosophy, biblical and heroic subjects, and public occasions in an elevated, digressive manner, claiming the liberty of Pindaric inspiration.
narrative_structure: A group of irregular odes with varied line lengths and stanza forms, loosely modeled on (a mistaken idea of) Pindar's structure.
meter_and_prosody: Irregular line lengths and stanzas, giving the effect of inspired freedom — the 'Pindaric' that Dryden and others adopted.
historical_context: Published in Poems (1656); Cowley mistook Pindar's regular triadic form for inspired irregularity, but his 'Pindaric' became a fashionable English form for grand subjects.
literary_significance: Cowley's odes created the English Pindaric, used by Dryden ('Alexander's Feast'), Congreve, and the eighteenth-century ode-writers, and important in the history of the ode.
bibliographical_notes: Published in Poems (1656). Standard edition: The Poems of Abraham Cowley (A. R. Waller, ed., Cambridge).

title: The Mistress
alternative_titles: The Mistress; or, Several Copies of Love-Verses
description: The long sequence of love poems in Cowley's Poems (1656), a display of metaphysical wit and conceit on an idealised, largely fictitious mistress, which Johnson cited for its 'violence' of conceit but which shows Cowley's command of the amorous lyric.
plot_or_argument: The poems court and lament an unnamed mistress through elaborate conceits of love's pain, hope, and constancy, more an exercise of wit than a record of a real attachment.
narrative_structure: A loose sequence of love lyrics united by the conceit of the unattainable mistress.
meter_and_prosody: Varied lyric meters with dense metaphysical conceits and witty argument.
historical_context: Published in Poems (1656); Johnson's Life of Cowley famously quoted it as an example of the metaphysical 'violence' of conceit, by which he meant the yoking of heterogeneous ideas.
literary_significance: A representative and influential work of metaphysical love poetry, central to Johnson's definition of the 'metaphysical' wit and to later understanding of the school.
attribution_notes: Uncontested; the identity of 'the mistress' is thought to be largely fictitious.
bibliographical_notes: Published in Poems (1656). Standard edition: The Poems of Abraham Cowley (A. R. Waller, ed., Cambridge).

title: Essays in Verse and Prose
description: Cowley's posthumous essays (1668) — 'Of Myself', 'Of Solitude', 'Of Gardens', 'Of Liberty', 'Of the Late Civil War', and 'Of Plants' — which champion retirement, the country life, and the new experimental philosophy, and helped establish the familiar, conversational English essay.
plot_or_argument: The essays reflect on retirement and the value of solitude, the love of gardening and the countryside, liberty, the recent Civil Wars, and the Royal Society's programme, in a personal, digressive, hortatory manner.
narrative_structure: A collection of familiar essays, some with verse interspersed, on moral and philosophical subjects.
meter_and_prosody: Graceful, conversational prose with occasional verse; a cultivated, reflective tone.
historical_context: Written after Cowley's retirement to Chertsey following the Restoration and published posthumously in 1668; 'Of Plants' is an Englishing of his Latin De Plantis and engages the new science.
literary_significance: Cowley's essays shaped the Restoration familiar essay and the ideal of cultivated retirement, influencing Steele, Addison, and Johnson, and linked literature to the Royal Society's ideals.
bibliographical_notes: Published 1668. Standard edition: The Essays and Other Prose Writings of Abraham Cowley (A. B. Gough, ed., Oxford).
